source: Sagiv, Akam, Witten, Daw (2025) Between planning and map building: prioritizing replay when future goals are uncertain. Neuron
finding: Replay builds a goal-general map called the Geodesic Representation (GR): one Q-table per candidate goal, learned off-policy. Replay priority is need times gain, averaged over beliefs about which goals will matter. Value replay (Mattar and Daw) is the special case of one goal.
numbers: GR is a stack of Q-value pages, one per goal state, each with unit reward at that goal. One transition s to s' updates all goals at once. Priority = expected gain over P(g) of H_post minus H_pre.
quote: replay builds a set of value functions: one for each potential goal
limits: Tabular only. Gain is computed by brute-force enumeration. Goal beliefs are hand-built per task, not learned by one general rule. No new animal data.
agent_relevance: Memory design: store routes (sub-solutions) for several likely future goals, and rank what to rehearse by (how likely the goal is) x (how much the update improves reaching it).

source: Sagiv, Akam, Witten, Daw (2025) Between planning and map building: prioritizing replay when future goals are uncertain. Neuron
finding: Asymmetric T-maze simulation: a Q-value agent replays only the path to the nearest reward and stops. The GR agent replays paths from both goals, in order of distance.
numbers: Single simulated example (Fig 2a). Reward arms are terminal and are candidate goals. No statistics.
limits: Stylised. Assumes a known start state and no online exploration.
agent_relevance: A single-goal memory stops after the nearest solution. A goal-general memory keeps the far alternative too. Cheap to add for a few known candidate goals.

source: Sagiv, Akam, Witten, Daw (2025) Between planning and map building: prioritizing replay when future goals are uncertain. Neuron
finding: GR replay favours bottleneck states. Its need term equals a discounted betweenness centrality. But corridor interiors are replayed less than their centrality predicts, because one replay bridges many paths.
numbers: Two mazes: two rooms joined by a corridor, and a four-room community graph. Mean state replay over n=250 simulated sequences each.
limits: Model prediction only. No animal data was run against the bottleneck prediction in this paper.
agent_relevance: Store and rehearse shared sub-steps (bottlenecks, shared lemmas) that many goals route through, rather than goal-specific tails.

source: Sagiv, Akam, Witten, Daw (2025) Between planning and map building: prioritizing replay when future goals are uncertain. Neuron
finding: Model reproduces the lagging replay of Gillespie et al. 2021: previous-block goal arm over-replayed, current-goal replay rises over the repeat phase, and the old goal fades over several blocks. The Q-value agent predicts the opposite (prefers the current goal, declines within a block).
numbers: Eight-arm task. Roughly ten blocks per goal in the whole experiment. Two Rescorla-Wagner processes: fast R_behav for choice, slow R_replay for the across-block goal distribution. Match is qualitative (replotted data next to simulation curves); no fit statistic reported.
limits: Key assumption: replay uses a slow recency-weighted goal prior. Free parameters (learning rates, forgetting, replay budget) set by hand. Qualitative match only.
agent_relevance: Keep two goal trackers: a fast one for what we pursue now, a slow one for which goals recur. Let the slow one decide what to rehearse.

source: Sagiv, Akam, Witten, Daw (2025) Between planning and map building: prioritizing replay when future goals are uncertain. Neuron
finding: Model also reproduces Carey et al. 2019: behaviour followed the deprived outcome but replay favoured the other arm. Q-value replay predicts matched behaviour and replay.
numbers: Rats had only two or three sessions per goal to estimate the goal distribution. The goal-level learning rate was assumed to be appropriately calibrated.
limits: Simulation only, one learning rate chosen to fit. Cannot separate this from other accounts of motivational-state effects.
agent_relevance: Present motivation or the current objective should not fully set what gets rehearsed. Keep records for the alternative branch too.

source: Sagiv, Akam, Witten, Daw (2025) Between planning and map building: prioritizing replay when future goals are uncertain. Neuron
finding: Same model reproduces Pfeiffer and Foster style predictive replay (replay toward the Home well, no preference for the previous Random well) when the agent is given the true alternating goal dynamics. This is why value-like replay appears in some tasks.
numbers: 6x6 grid of 35 wells, one Home well per session. Home-containing replays gave larger expected improvement in Home navigation than other replays (Fig 5c). Home replay from trial 2 (Fig 5b).
limits: Here goal beliefs were set to the true dynamics by hand, not learned. So the model can fit both patterns by choosing the prior. This is a flexibility risk, not an independent test.
agent_relevance: Which regime applies depends on goal statistics: one dominant stable goal with a big route space gives planning for now. Several rotating goals gives map building.

source: Sagiv, Akam, Witten, Daw (2025) Between planning and map building: prioritizing replay when future goals are uncertain. Neuron
finding: Untested predictions: replay order should depend on how soon and how often each goal is expected. With p11=0.5 the GR agent replays g1 then g2. With p11=0.05 it replays g2 first. Replay should occur before any reward in latent learning. An every-trial rotating Gillespie variant should give predictive replay.
numbers: Simulated detour task with a Markov goal process, p11 = 0.5 vs 0.05.
limits: No empirical test yet. Author-stated.
agent_relevance: Gives a rule a scaffold can copy: order rehearsal by expected recurrence of each goal, not only by the active goal.

source: Sagiv, Akam, Witten, Daw (2025) Between planning and map building: prioritizing replay when future goals are uncertain. Neuron
finding: Boundary conditions named by the authors: prioritisation matters only when experience and replay are limited. Value replay wins when one goal predominates for long, the route space is large, and the animal knows the dynamics. Rival or related accounts: Temporal Context Model replay (Zhou et al.), Bakermans et al., Chen and van der Meer.
numbers: Not applicable (discussion section).
limits: TCM replay makes similar predictions because TCM associations coincide with the SR (the need term). They differ mainly where gain matters.
agent_relevance: If compute is cheap, no prioritisation is needed. For a budget-limited agent, prioritisation by expected future use is justified.

source: Gillespie et al. (2021) Hippocampal replay reflects specific past experiences rather than a plan for subsequent choice. Neuron
finding: Rats on an 8-arm win-stay lose-switch task. Pre-choice remote replay was enriched for the previous block's goal arm, not the upcoming choice. The arm just visited was under-replayed.
numbers: 4 rats, 30-tetrode CA1 arrays. Remote replay was 35.1%, 41.1%, 34.5%, 47.2% of SWRs per rat. Previous-goal arm made up roughly 20% of pre-choice remote events in search trials. GLM: about 2-fold rate increase for the previous goal arm. Future arm: small increase, significant in 2 of 4 rats in the subset analysis and 3 of 4 in the GLM. Past arm: reduced.
quote: far fewer replays of the immediate past arm than would be expected by chance
limits: Only 4 animals, well-trained, forward and reverse not separated. Mixed events are common. Shows content only, not what replay later does to behaviour.
agent_relevance: The finding that drives the map account. For an agent: rehearsal of a stale goal is not necessarily a bug, but it can lag the active goal.

source: Gillespie et al. (2021), repeat-phase and sample details
finding: The pattern was the same in the repeat phase when the goal was known. Replay of the previous goal stayed the strongest single-arm effect, and other arms together were the majority of replay.
numbers: Repeat trials: n = 1347, 1661, 1154, 1730 per rat. Search trials: 711, 848, 725, 1065. Sessions: 24, 32, 23, 33. Chance reward rate 0.125. Blocks per rat: 89, 85, 105, 166.
limits: Rules out the simple explanation that no goal was known during search. Does not rule out a slow goal-prior account (which is what Sagiv proposes).
agent_relevance: Replay was spread over many arms, consistent with maintaining a map across goals rather than one plan.

source: Gillespie et al. (2021), interpretation
finding: The paper frames the choice as planning versus memory maintenance and reads the lag as favouring maintenance. Sagiv et al. later argue the same data fit a prioritised-map account.
numbers: Design compared replay on trials with and without specific arm choices; no extra figure extracted here.
limits: Competing explanations persist: consolidation, recency and map building all fit.
agent_relevance: Do not read lag as failure. Judge any rehearsal scheme by whether it helps later tasks, not only the current one.

source: Carey et al. (2019) Reward revaluation biases hippocampal replay content away from the preferred outcome. Nature Neuroscience
finding: T-maze with food and water. Rats shifted behaviour toward the restricted outcome, but replay shifted away from it. The effect appeared before task experience each day and did not reverse with experience.
numbers: Numbers not recorded (abstract only, read through Europe PMC). Europe PMC showed 87 citations.
limits: Abstract only. Journal and exact author list not verified in this read.
agent_relevance: Motivation can decouple behaviour from rehearsal content. Keep records for the non-preferred outcome too.

source: Mattar and Daw (2018) Prioritized memory access explains planning and hippocampal replay. Nature Neuroscience
finding: Replay priority = gain x need. Prioritised replay speeds learning over random Dyna and a model-free agent. It yields forward and reverse sequences and asymmetric effects of positive and negative prediction errors. Sagiv et al. generalise it to many goals.
numbers: Linear track and 2D obstacle field simulations. Utility = expected increase in future reward from one Bellman backup. The need term gives depth-first sequences.
limits: Tabular simulations, gain by brute force. Cannot explain lagging replay (the gap Sagiv fills).
agent_relevance: Prioritising by expected use and expected improvement is the base rule for any memory-rehearsal scheduler.

source: Pfeiffer and Foster (2013) Hippocampal place-cell sequences depict future paths to remembered goals. Nature
finding: Before goal-directed navigation in an open arena, hippocampal sequences ran from the current location toward the known goal and predicted immediate behaviour, even for novel start-goal pairs.
numbers: Numbers not recorded (abstract only). Europe PMC showed 934 citations.
limits: Abstract only. Replay was biased to a Home well visited every trial; Sagiv argue this is the single-dominant-goal regime.
agent_relevance: Evidence for the value end: when one goal dominates, rehearse routes to it.

source: Widloski and Foster (2022) Flexible rerouting of hippocampal replay sequences around changing barriers in the absence of global place field remapping. Neuron
finding: Replays depicted new goal-directed paths around moved barriers and largely avoided barrier violations. This was learned rapidly and without place-cell remapping.
numbers: In 27 of 31 barrier sessions (87%) barrier conformity beat the 95th percentile of control (binomial p<0.001). 37 sessions from rats 1-3; up to 295 cells. Rate maps stable in 1,686 of 2,887 comparisons (58%); population vectors stable in 28,788 of 33,245 (87%).
limits: 3 rats for replay analysis. Goals were also moved, so it cannot tell whether replay served the current goal or all goals.
agent_relevance: Rehearsed routes must respect updated constraints. Re-plan around new blockers before storing routes.

source: Chen and van der Meer (2024, version dated 2026) Paradoxical replay can protect contextual task representations from destructive interference when experience is unbalanced. bioRxiv
finding: Rival account of paradoxical (lagging) replay. In a network with rich task-specific representations, unbalanced experience degraded them, and replay of non-chosen options reversed it. Lazy networks did not degrade. In two rat datasets, richer hippocampal task representations went with more paradoxical replay.
numbers: Rich vs lazy hidden-unit distance differed (p<0.001, Wilcoxon). Rat data: representational separation vs paradoxical replay r=0.53 (single-cell) and r=0.49 (ensemble), both p<0.05. Second analysis: r=0.55 (p<0.05) for single-cell, but ensemble r=0.32, p=0.18 (not significant). Text extracted from a PDF with garbled spacing, so values are as read.
limits: Preprint, not peer reviewed at the time. Correlational, few sessions. Authors give no mechanism for how the hippocampus knows what to replay.
agent_relevance: A second reason to rehearse the non-chosen option: protect against interference when experience is lopsided. Rehearse neglected branches too.

source: Diekmann and Cheng (2023) A model of hippocampal replay driven by experience and environmental structure facilitates spatial learning. eLife
finding: Rival cheap account: a stochastic replay mechanism prioritised by experience strength, experience similarity and inhibition of return. It trains RL agents far better than random replay and nearly as well as the costly Mattar and Daw algorithm.
numbers: Numeric comparison not extracted (abstract and intro read).
limits: Does not model future-goal beliefs. Author names are from memory, not verified on the page.
agent_relevance: A low-compute heuristic (strength, similarity, inhibition of return) may approximate prioritised rehearsal when exact gain is too costly.

source: Bakermans et al. (2025) Constructing future behavior in the hippocampal formation through composition and replay
finding: Compositional state-space model: replay from newly found landmarks creates new remote firing fields, and when the landmark moves, replay builds a new field at the same vector. Agents act well in new environments by composing primitives. Sagiv et al. note it has replay building paths to goals but no goal-switching statistics.
numbers: Two datasets. Example sample sizes: n=753 (home) vs 1,143 (elsewhere); n=6,860 home vs 20,912 elsewhere spikes.
limits: Journal name and full author list not checked against the page. Model-heavy.
agent_relevance: Supports reusing primitives across goals rather than storing whole plans.

source: Exploring replay (2025), normative account of exploratory replay
finding: Extends Mattar and Daw's replay theory to uncertain environments, deriving approximately optimal exploratory replay choices and predictions in a navigation task.
numbers: Binomial tests are used against data; no single headline number extracted.
limits: Authors not recorded. Addresses exploration under uncertainty, not multiple future goals.
agent_relevance: Rehearsal should also target uncertain parts of the map, not only known high-value routes.

source: Spatial learning drives rapid goal representation in hippocampal ripples without place field accumulation or goal-oriented theta sequences (2022)
finding: During active navigation the hippocampal network showed no goal enrichment (no place-field accumulation, no goal-oriented theta sequences). But in brief pauses before movement, a novel goal location emerged rapidly in ripples.
numbers: Unit n=8 sessions x 4 time points per group. Several ANOVA effects were non-significant (p=0.25, 0.60, 0.99 for the factors listed).
limits: Authors and journal not recorded. Supports a goal-representation role of ripples (value side), at odds with a pure map view.
agent_relevance: Goal-specific rehearsal in pauses before acting is real. Do both: rehearse the current goal before acting, and keep a wider map in the background.

source: Carta et al. (2024) SAC-GLAM: Improving online RL for LLM agents with Soft Actor-Critic and Hindsight Relabeling. arXiv 2410.12481
finding: Off-policy replay with hindsight goal relabeling for LLM agents. Adding HER (relabel failed trajectories with goals they reached) made SAC-GLAM more sample efficient.
numbers: Exact scores not extracted. The paper says that with HER SAC-GLAM becomes even more sample efficient and reaches comparable performance in training time.
quote: even more sample efficient and achieves comparable performance in terms of training time
limits: First author name from memory, not verified. Trains small LLMs online. A training method, not an inference-time scaffold.
agent_relevance: HER is the AI cousin of the GR idea: reuse experience for goals other than the one pursued.

source: Li et al. (2026) Spinning Straw into Gold: Relabeling LLM Agent Trajectories in Hindsight for Successful Demonstrations (HSL). ICLR 2026
finding: An auxiliary LLM relabels each finished trajectory with all the natural-language goals actually achieved, then trains on these. Gains were large on ALFWorld.
numbers: Table 1 (Llama-3.2-1B agent, Llama-3.3-70B relabeler). Columns read as ALFWorld seen / ALFWorld unseen / PlanCraft / WebShop: SFT 82.14 / 78.36 / 70.00 / 63.81; SFT+HSL 93.57 / 97.76 / 75.12 / 66.97; DPO 85.71 / 82.84 / 71.25 / 69.54; DPO+HSL 92.86 / 94.78 / 75.42 / 70.52. Authors state 8% to 32% success gain on ALFWorld.
limits: Column labels were read from a flattened table. Small agent model. Run-to-run variance not checked. Fine-tuning, not scaffold use.
agent_relevance: Direct support for the idea that a trajectory is also a route to other goals. Matches the map-over-goals view.

source: Li et al. (2026) HSL sample efficiency and boundary condition
finding: HSL beat baselines trained on the full data while using about a quarter of the demonstrations. Gains were smaller where only one goal is achievable per task (WebShop) and larger with long tasks and many valid goals.
numbers: ALFWorld unseen: 800 demos SFT 55.2% vs SFT+HSL 83.6%. DPO with over 3,200 demos 82.8% vs DPO+HSL with 800 demos 92.5%. WebShop SFT 63.81 to 66.97.
limits: Agrees with the Sagiv boundary: one dominant goal means little gain from goal-general reuse. Numbers read from a flattened chart text.
agent_relevance: Worth the extra memory machinery only when tasks have many plausible goals or sub-goals.

source: Ding (2026) AgentHER: Hindsight Experience Replay for LLM Agent Trajectory Relabeling. arXiv 2603.21357
finding: Relabels failed agent trajectories with the goal they actually achieved, then trains. Improves over success-only SFT on WebArena and ToolBench across four model families.
numbers: +7.1 to +11.7 pp over SFT-Success. 2x data efficiency (matches baseline with 50% of successful demos). +5.8 to +9.2 pp from 1.5B to 72B (peak +9.2 at 14B). +9.5 pp zero-shot transfer from WebArena to ToolBench. Qwen2.5-7B WebArena gain +8.9 pp over SFT-Success 18.9%.
limits: Single author, preprint, one lab. Gains measured against its own baselines. Fine-tuning, not inference-time memory.
agent_relevance: Failed runs contain correct partial solutions for other goals. Store them tagged by the goal they do solve.

source: Ding (2026) AgentHER: label quality and failure types
finding: Quality gating is the critical component. Relabel precision 94.1% with one judge and 97.7% with multi-judge verification (noise 5.9% to 2.3%). Without gating, noise rises to 14.8%. Most gain from incomplete runs (+11.2 pp) and constraint violations (+9.8 pp); least from tool errors (+2.1 pp).
numbers: Human check of 200 pairs; 31 filtered out, 38.7% of those were actually valid. GPT-4o 14.3% on WebArena.
limits: Judge-based labels can be wrong. Noise matters more than volume.
agent_relevance: If the agent relabels its own failed routes with other goals, verify the claimed goal against evidence in the trace before storing.

source: Hindsight Planner: a closed-loop few-shot planner for embodied instruction following (2024). arXiv 2412.19562
finding: Uses hindsight prompting to relabel suboptimal rollouts into completed tasks, at inference time, for an LLM planner.
numbers: Not opened beyond the search-result description. No numbers recorded.
limits: Only a search-result description was seen. Authors and results unverified.
agent_relevance: A prompt-level (not training) use of hindsight relabeling. Worth a follow-up read.

source: Search note: LLM tests of map versus value replay
finding: No LLM or AI study was found that tests the map-versus-value replay prediction directly (replay ordering by goal-recurrence beliefs). The nearest AI work is hindsight goal relabeling (HER, AgentHER, HSL, SAC-GLAM).
numbers: Searches: 3 WebSearch calls plus Europe PMC. Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate-limited and the arXiv API returned nothing, so coverage is incomplete.
limits: Absence of evidence in a limited search. Original HER (Andrychowicz 2017), Prioritized ER (Schaul 2016) and Kaelbling 1993 were not opened.
agent_relevance: A rehearsal-by-goal-recurrence rule in a scaffold would be a new test, not a replication.
